assignment: Monte Carlo/MCMC: rejection, importance sampling, control variates, error and CLTs, Metropolis-Hastings/Gibbs, ergodicity/mixing, HMC/Langevin numerical bias, adaptive MCMC conditions, and diagnostic limitations.
extraction: PDF text extracted with MuPDF mutool draw -F txt. PDF page images were not transcribed. The extraction contains occasional missing math glyphs; claims were checked against the supplied PDF at the cited section where notation was material. No source text was copied into the dossier.

sources.author: Art B. Owen
sources.read_status: Relevant unit complete: Chapter 2 §§2.1-2.3, printed pp. 15-22. Chapter 2 Theorem 2.1 states the IID CLT but cites Chung for its proof; the library's existing local IID CLT proof is the proof route instead. Other Chapter 2 sections were not used.
anchors: §2.2 IID CLT and plug-in standard error

sources.author: Art B. Owen
sources.read_status: Relevant unit complete: §4.7, printed pp. 21-26, including Algorithms 4.5-4.6 and Theorems 4.2-4.5 with their displayed proofs. Other Chapter 4 units were not used.

sources.title: Monte Carlo theory, methods and examples, Chapter 8: Variance reduction
sources.author: Art B. Owen
sources.read_status: Relevant unit complete: §8.9, printed pp. 28-32. The fixed-coefficient scalar and vector variance calculations are shown; the same-sample estimated-coefficient bias is analyzed to order O_p(n^-1), and an independent pilot estimate is distinguished. Other Chapter 8 sections were not used.

sources.title: Monte Carlo theory, methods and examples, Chapter 9: Importance sampling
sources.author: Art B. Owen
sources.read_status: Relevant units complete: §§9.1-9.3, printed pp. 4-13, and §9.10, printed pp. 25-27. Theorem 9.1 has a proof; Theorem 9.2 proves consistency by the strong law. Theorem 9.4 for estimated control coefficients cites Owen-Zhou (2000) instead of proving it, so a local derivation is still required if included.
anchors: §9.1 support, unbiased estimator, exact variance and infinite-variance failures

sources.title: Monte Carlo theory, methods and examples, Chapters 11-12: Markov chain Monte Carlo and Gibbs sampler
sources.author: Art B. Owen
sources.read_status: Relevant units complete: §§11.2-11.4, printed pp. 8-20; §§11.10-11.13, pp. 37-41; and §§12.1, 12.4, pp. 49-55. Several finite-state convergence/LLN proofs are citations to Norris or Levin-Peres-Wilmer; the general-state proofs are supplied by S06. Gibbs invariance is derived, with the direct detailed-balance calculation restricted to discrete full conditionals.

sources.title: General state space Markov chains and MCMC algorithms
sources.author: Gareth O. Roberts and Jeffrey S. Rosenthal
sources.read_status: Relevant units complete: §2, source PDF pp. 4-10; §§3.1-3.5, pp. 11-28; §§4.1-4.6, pp. 29-41; and §§5.1-5.4, pp. 42-51. Proof qualifications: Theorem 4's coupling proof uses the cited Jain-Jameson small-set theorem without proving it; Theorem 9 uses the cited petite-set-to-small-set theorem without proving it; Theorem 25 uses a cited L2 operator-norm equivalence. These are outstanding source-level proof dependencies for any local claim that copies those routes.
anchors: §5.1-5.4 Markov-chain CLT counterexample, sufficient conditions and Poisson equation route

sources.title: On the Markov chain central limit theorem
sources.author: Galin L. Jones
sources.read_status: Relevant units complete: §§1-4 through Theorem 9, source PDF pp. 1-14. These sections connect TV/geometric drift rates to alpha/rho/phi mixing and state the precise CLT hypotheses; classical mixing CLT proofs are cited, while the implication from geometric TV rates to the strong-mixing hypothesis is proved in the paper. Remaining application examples/appendix material was not used.
anchors: Theorem 9 summary of alternatives and failure of finite variance alone

sources.title: MCMC using Hamiltonian dynamics
sources.author: Radford M. Neal
sources.publication: Chapter 5 in Handbook of Markov Chain Monte Carlo (2011), 113-162
sources.read_status: Relevant units complete: §§2.1-2.3, source PDF pp. 3-10; §§3.1-3.2, pp. 11-15; §4.2, pp. 23-26; and §5.2, pp. 37-39. Leapfrog reversibility/volume preservation is proved by shear-map calculations; the HMC invariance proof is an informal equal-volume partition argument, not a measure-theoretic proof. The remaining examples/extensions were not used.
anchors: §2.3 leapfrog equations, reversibility, volume preservation and O(epsilon^2) global error
§5.2 one-step LMC/MALA and asymmetric MH correction

sources.title: Non-asymptotic convergence analysis for the Unadjusted Langevin Algorithm
sources.author: Alain Durmus and Éric Moulines
sources.read_status: Relevant units complete: §1, §2 including Theorem 10 and its §4.6 proof, §3.3 including Theorem 21, §4.12 proof of Proposition 20, and §5.1 proof of Theorem 21. Theorem 10 uses gradient-Lipschitz L1 plus the superexponential Lyapunov tail condition H1 and proves a constant-step stationary law pi_gamma with a nonzero O(sqrt(gamma)) V-TV bias bound; its proof cites external diffusion-contraction results and leaves the final bound A to 'similar lines'. Theorem 21 gives finite-time convergence conditions under strongly-convex-outside-a-ball H3; its proof also invokes external diffusion-coupling bounds. Other regimes/proofs were not used.

sources.title: Coupling and Ergodicity of Adaptive MCMC Algorithms
sources.author: Gareth O. Roberts and Jeffrey S. Rosenthal
sources.read_status: Relevant units complete: §§1-10, source PDF pp. 1-24. Proofs read for the simultaneous-uniform-ergodicity plus diminishing-adaptation theorem, the nonuniform bounded-in-probability convergence-time (containment) theorem, the simultaneous drift/minorization corollary, and bounded-function WLLN. The paper gives counterexamples to stationarity/convergence and to strong LLN under its weak theorem. No adaptive CLT is established.
anchors: §5 Theorem 5: simultaneous uniform ergodicity plus diminishing adaptation
§6 Theorem 13: diminishing adaptation plus convergence times bounded in probability
§9 Theorem 23 bounded-function WLLN and Example 24 strong-law failure
